rv.q: It doesn't quite work though, in large part because it doesn't make a convincing argument for why this story needs this treatment.
True, there is a brief glimpse of a vehicle at the very start; flashing headlights and flowing lines of LEDs along the walls evoke motion on the highway later on.

The overall effect is a solid and occasionally charming musical which eschews whimsy in favour of real life jeopardy, and is a female buddy tale which comes close to emulating the shenanigans of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.

It is, however, an unusual choice. Not because of the story itself, but because this is fundamentally a road movie, with much of the action taking place in a moving car, something that presents obvious theatrical challenges. In an interview published in the programme, Khouri describes the musical as a “completely new iteration” of the story.

Yet bringing it to the stage falls flat. The best jokes, the smartest lines, and the power of this feminist parable all come direct from the movie, that made stars of Susan Sarandon, Geena Davis and a very young Brad Pitt. Their stage incarnations are excellent.
Thelma & Louise's road trip keeps going for ever – but now it's destined to continue as a terrific musical.
It's funny, emotional, uplifting and defiant – with two phenomenal performances from its brilliant Thelma and Louise.
